newsitem.title: UK: British Conservatives face new rift over Europe.
newsitem.headline: British Conservatives face new rift over Europe.

text.p: Britain's ruling Conservatives were plunged into disarray on Wednesday when Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind said that on balance the government was hostile to a single currency for the European Union.
The remark, made in a BBC radio interview, ruptured a carefully brokered Cabinet agreement of studied neutrality on the issue ahead of an election likely on May 1.
Finance minister Kenneth Clarke, the most pro-European of Prime Minister John Major's senior colleagues, said Rifkind had made "a slip of the tongue".
But Rifkind, just hours later, stood by his comment, delighting so-called Eurosceptics in the ruling party.

"On balance we are hostile to a single currency, but we accept you have to think very carefully about these matters before you rule them out completely," said Rifkind, who has become steadily more Eurosceptic in recent months. He later passed up an opportunity to calm the controversy by saying he did not regret using the word "hostile".
"I don't regret it because, in the context in which I was using it, it made sense and it was consistent with what the government's policy is," he said.
The Conservatives' opponents pounced on Rifkind's remarks.
"You have got government ministers at sixes and sevens...it is a quite extraordinary situation," said opposition Labour leader Tony Blair.
"The government can't sustain a position on Europe for a week," Paddy Ashdown, leader of the minority Liberal Democrats, Britain's most pro-European party, told reporters.
Rifkind made his remarks in Bonn ahead of a speech on Britain's attitude to the European Union in which he emphasised the need to guard against centralisation of power to Brussels.

The single currency is a nightmare issue for Major because of the conflict within his party between ministers such as Clarke who believe Britain should join provided it is properly set up and MPs who have set their face completely against it and distrust anything that emanates from Brussels.

A government line had appeared agreed when Rifkind and Clarke emerged from a cabinet meeting last month to declare that while Britain would keeping its options open, it was unlikely to join up if the currency went ahead as planned in January 1999.
Following Rifkind's remark and Clarke's dismissal of it, Major was left to attempt to paper over the differences.
He told journalists the government would need to be persuaded that it was "positively beneficial" to join a single currency before it would do so.
"We would need to be persuaded that it was better. We are not so persuaded at the moment," he said.

John Redwood, a Eurosceptic right-winger who resigned from the cabinet in 1995 to challenge Major for the party leadership, said he believed Rifkind's statement was a key gain for those on the Eurosceptic side of the argument.
"He clearly changed the line from the one we heard before," he said. "I find that most encouraging."

Major was already facing formidable problems in holding his party together on the single currency before Rifkind spoke. Up to 150 Conservative candidates at the election are planning to openly oppose it in their election addresses to voters.
The disarray is hindering Major's efforts to use a buoyant economy to eliminate an 18 percent lead currently enjoyed by Labour in the opinion polls.
